name: GPU, web and parallel renderers
text:
# GPU, web and parallel renderers
## Overview
This family covers rendering systems that map volumetric data $I(x,y,z)$ to perceptible outputs by offloading computation to parallel hardware (GPUs, multi-core CPUs) or executing entirely within web browsers via WebGL/WebGPU [S1][S3, unofficial]. It addresses the computational intensity of volume rendering by leveraging massive parallelism for tasks like [ray casting](#6080-ray-casting.md), [splatting](#23-splatting.md), and data sorting [S1, S2]. It is distinguished from [Voxel engines and games](47-voxel-engines-and-games.md) by its focus on general-purpose visualization rather than game engine integration, and from [Film and production rendering](48-film-and-production-rendering.md) by its emphasis on real-time or near-real-time interactivity and web compatibility [G].

## Shared principles
This family builds on the shared principles of [Systems and applications](46-systems-and-applications.md).

## Subtopics

### [WebSplatter](1741-websplatter.md)
[WebSplatter](#1741-websplatter.md) is a WebGPU-based renderer for [3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)](#1174-3d-gaussian-splatting-3dgs.md) designed to achieve high-performance, cross-device compatibility in web browsers. It solves the problem of unstable and memory-intensive [Gaussian Splatting](#946-gaussian-splatting.md) implementations on the web by replacing CPU-based and spin-wait-based sorting with a wait-free GPU [radix sort](#10404-radix-sort-gpu.md) and optimizing memory access patterns. Unlike sibling methods that rely on WebGL or naive WebGPU ports, WebSplatter ensures stability on low-end mobile hardware and avoids the busy-waiting pitfalls of Apple M-series chips, maintaining visual fidelity comparable to native [CUDA](#3671-dual-contouring-2d-cuda.md) implementations. Choose this method when targeting stable, high-fidelity 3DGS in web environments across diverse hardware.

### [ClearView (Unified) Renderer](2460-clearview-unified-renderer.md)
ClearView (Unified) is a 3-pass WebGL2 renderer designed for visualizing unstructured hexahedral meshes, specifically wireframes and scalar fields, by adapting GPU-accelerated parallel prefix list (PPLL) techniques to browser constraints. It solves the problem of rendering complex volumetric meshes in WebGL2, which lacks Shader Storage Buffer Objects (SSBOs), by encoding mesh data into `image2D` textures and using [atomic operations](#3684-atomic-operations-for-global-counters.md) to manage fragment accumulation. Unlike [WebSplatter](1741-websplatter.md) which focuses on splatting, ClearView explicitly handles hexahedral topology via a gather-resolve pipeline that supports depth-sorted [alpha blending](#5750-alpha-blending.md) without CPU-side sorting. Choose this method when rendering hexahedral meshes in WebGL2 without CPU-side sorting.

### [CPU-Driven Task Spawning](4397-cpu-driven-task-spawning.md)
[CPU-driven task spawning](#4397-cpu-driven-task-spawning.md) is a GPU execution model where the [CPU](#10688-naive-sdf-generation-cpu.md) acts as the central governor, deciding when and how GPU tasks are launched, while the GPU functions as a coprocessor that executes work requests but cannot generate new ones. This approach centralizes decision-making logic but suffers from high CPU-GPU communication latency, making it ineffective for pipelines with fine-grain micro-dependencies or stages that dynamically compute the work for subsequent stages. It differs from GPU-driven spawning (where the GPU generates its own work) and [asynchronous submission](#5531-asynchronous-submission.md) (which hides latency but still relies on CPU-initiated commands) by strictly enforcing a top-down control hierarchy. Choose this method when centralized CPU control is required, but avoid it for fine-grain dynamic workloads.

### [Pure client-side renderers](5040-pure-client-side-renderers.md)
[Pure client-side renderers](#5040-pure-client-side-renderers.md) perform all volume rendering computations within the user's web browser, requiring only a file server as a backend to serve volumetric data. This approach eliminates the need for dedicated rendering servers or backend gradient computation, shifting the processing load entirely to the client's GPU. It is distinguished from server-side rendering architectures by its reliance on local execution and from hybrid models by the absence of server-side rasterization or ray-marching services. Choose this method when avoiding dedicated rendering servers or backend services is a priority.

### [Single Node Multi-GPU/Server Architecture](5165-single-node-multi-gpu-server-architecture.md)
This architecture enables interactive visualization of large volumetric datasets on resource-constrained mobile clients by offloading all rendering computation to a server-side cluster. It differs from pure client-side renderers by requiring a dedicated rendering backend, and from distributed shared-memory schemes by utilizing a single node with multiple GPUs/CPUs or a cluster of nodes managed via the Chromium framework. It solves the problem of limited local hardware (e.g., PDAs) by transmitting compressed image buffers rather than raw volumetric data. Choose this method when client hardware is insufficient for local rendering but network transmission of compressed frames is viable.

### [CPU Multithreaded Rendering](6052-cpu-multithreaded-rendering.md)
CPU multithreaded rendering manages [parallel chunk rendering](#3994-chunk-based-parallel-voxel-culling-rendering.md) using a thread pool pattern with a free renderer queue, active renderer counter, and condition variable synchronization. It differs from GPU-driven approaches by handling all scheduling and synchronization on the CPU, making it suitable for CPU-bound voxel worlds that use Z-buffering to prevent overdraw. Choose this method for CPU-based chunked rendering where thread pool management is preferred over GPU compute shaders.

### Multi-GPU Load Balancing
Create a GL-Context on both X-screens (for multiple NVidia cards) and switch rendering between them one time per frame [S1]. Combine results of both cards. Since the second card's result is combined with the first, the second card need not be connected to a monitor [S1]. Split the sorted array of voxels equally over both cards by interleaving detail coefficients (and histogram) for each pyramid level [S1]. Combine resulting images using a pixel-wise maximum operator [S1]. The preferred pixel format for CPU transfer is `GL_UNSIGNED_INT_8_8_8_8` [S1]. No extension exists for direct data shuffling between cards; intermediate results must pass through the CPU using `glReadPixels` on one context and `glDrawPixels` on the other [S1]. Multi-threading rendering loops for multiple contexts did not yield performance gains because the algorithm is GPU-bound; CPU synchronization overhead outweighs the tiny load [S1]. Interleaving coefficients is preferred over splitting in the middle to better divide load during [progressive refinement](#11267-temporal-and-progressive-rendering.md) [S1].

### Concurrent CUDA Streams for VR
A VR optimization that concurrently runs CUDA kernels for the left and right eye in multiple streams to better utilize the GPU and mitigate under-utilization caused by imbalanced workloads (varying amounts of splats per tile) [S2]. Overlapping rendering pipelines for left and right eyes in VR using separate, non-blocking CUDA streams fills GPU utilization gaps caused by imbalanced workloads [S2]. The right eye's tile ID sorting and rasterization stages are overlapped with the left eye's rasterization stage [S2]. Imbalanced workloads under-utilize the GPU because the stream waits until the kernel's longest-running thread-blocks are finished [S2]. The left and right eye's sorting stages must not be overlapped, as this would require creating separate intermediate sorting buffers, increasing memory usage [S2]. On the Berlin scene (1.0 M splats), a single stream takes 6.3 ms while concurrent streams take 5.2 ms. On the Campus scene (28.6 M splats), a single stream takes 16.2 ms while concurrent streams take 13.8 ms [S2].

### Web-Based Volume Rendering
In web-based environments, research focuses on solutions to network latency when loading volumetric data and improving volume rendering performance on the web [S3, unofficial]. Designed to work without a dedicated rendering backend and relies only on a file server. All volume rendering is done in the browser itself [S3, unofficial].

### Neuroglancer Multi-channel Rendering
Uses the same technique as Viv for representing multiple channels on the GPU ([accumulation-level intermixing](#5139-intermixing.md)) [S3, unofficial].

### Threaded Chunk Rendering
Manages parallel chunk rendering using a thread pool pattern with a free renderer queue, active renderer counter, and condition variable synchronization [S4, unofficial]. Iterate over loaded world chunks (i, j, k from 0 to LOADED_WORLD_SIZE). For each chunk, call renderChunk. In renderChunk, wait while activeRenderers >= MAX_RENDERERS and freeRenderers queue is empty. Pop a Renderer from freeRenderers or allocate a new one. Increment activeRenderers. Spawn a detached std::thread calling Chunk::render(chunk, renderer). When a renderer finishes, call freeRenderer to push it back to freeRenderers, decrement activeRenderers, and notify cv if activeRenderers reaches 0 [S4, unofficial]. MAX_RENDERERS is set to 20 (maximum concurrent rendering threads) [S4, unofficial]. RendererManager state includes `freeRenderers` (ThreadsafeQueue<Renderer*>), `cv` (std::condition_variable), `mtx` (std::mutex), and `activeRenderers` (std::atomic<int> initialized to 0) [S4, unofficial].

## Background
Web-based volume rendering research addresses network latency and browser performance, often relying on pure client-side architectures that require only a file server [S3, unofficial]. Early implementations focused on offloading rendering to [remote servers](#8196-remote-rendering-client-server-architecture.md), but modern approaches like WebSplatter and ClearView leverage WebGPU and WebGL2 for local computation [S1][S3, unofficial]. Multi-GPU techniques using NVidia drivers allow splitting workloads across cards via X-screens, though CPU-mediated data transfer remains a bottleneck [S1]. VR rendering optimizations utilize concurrent CUDA streams to overlap left/right eye rendering, improving utilization on imbalanced workloads [S2]. CPU-based multithreaded chunk rendering uses a thread pool with a maximum of 20 concurrent renderers to manage parallel world sections [S4, unofficial].
